title: Nonlocal transfer of quantized toroidal magnetic flux
abstract: We propose a nonlocal flux-transfer experiment in which a quantized magnetic-field excitation confined within one toroidal superconducting structure is coherently transferred to a spatially separated toroid without magnetic-field occupation of the intervening region. The transfer arises from quantized Aharonov-Bohm-type vector potential coupling mediated by a superconducting loop threading the toroids, which, however, remains in the ground state, acting only through a global fluxoid constraint. A direct experimental signature would be the observation of correlated, time-resolved flux exchange between remote toroids in a SQUID readout. We analyze an apparent signaling paradox related to this interaction as a probe of the broader question of whether spatiotemporal quantum coherence is fundamentally bounded. The proposed setup can provide an experimental testbed for addressing foundational questions such as the existence of an objective collapse of a wavefunction or the fundamental limits of macroscopic quantum coherence which is relevant to large scale quantum computers.
summary: This work proposes an experiment to transfer quantized magnetic flux nonlocally between superconducting toroids using only the global topological constraint. Theoretically, it develops a covariant master equation describing how long-range quantum coherence decays in such systems. It is significant because it connects measurable circuit physics to deep questions about wavefunction collapse and fundamental limits on quantum correlation.
main_problem: The paper proposes a nonlocal experiment to coherently transfer quantized magnetic flux between separated superconducting toroids, while simultaneously developing a covariant framework to test fundamental questions about spatiotemporal quantum coherence and wavefunction collapse.
main_result: The interaction is mediated by the global topological fluxoid constraint, leading to coupled normal modes. The theoretical development provides a gauge-invariant master equation describing decoherence based on condensate current rather than simple mass density localization.
method: The analysis combines solving classical equations of motion for coupled harmonic oscillators (flux qubits) with deriving and specializing a covariant collapse evolution equation from the Tomonaga–Schwinger formalism.
model_or_system: The system involves two toroidal superconducting structures linked by a common loop, modeled using fluxoid variables ($\hat{\Phi}$). The theoretical framework extends to a general covariant collapse law applied to condensate density matrices on a spacelike hypersurface.
key_observables: Correlated, time-resolved flux exchange between remote toroids; null measurement of magnetic-field leakage in the intervening region; mode splittings ($\Omega_{\pm}$); and the one-body density matrix $G^{(1)}(	heta, 	heta'; t)$.
important_parameters: Inductance ($L$), coupling strength ($J_{zz}$), collapse parameters ($\gamma_0$, $\chi_{	ext{cov}}$), and characteristic length scales ($\ell$).
main_assumptions: The nonlocal interaction is assumed to be mediated purely by the global fluxoid constraint, not local fields. The covariant collapse model is presented as a phenomenological extension of existing quantum mechanics.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from proposing the physical nonlocal experiment (flux transfer) using coupled harmonic oscillators, deriving the resulting Hamiltonian structure, and then generalizing this into a covariant quantum field theory framework to model coherence loss in the context of fundamental collapse mechanisms.
why_interesting: It bridges condensed matter physics (superconducting circuits) with foundational quantum foundations (collapse models), offering a tangible, measurable platform for testing abstract concepts like spatiotemporal coherence bounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of two toroidal superconducting flux elements interlinked by a common superconducting loop. The magnetic field of each toroid is confined to its core, while the linking loop is sensitive to the collective fluxoid in Eq. (1). The nonlocal transfer of the toroidal flux is mediated by a global fluxoid constraint imposed by the superconducting loop. Local SQUID detectors measure the toroidal fluxes, and field probes placed between the toroids perform a null test for the magnetic-field leakage.
